\chapter{Morning}
\label{ch:hi-morning}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say morning in Hindi and recognise \hi{सुबह} as a Persian-Arabic loan rather than a Sanskrit word.}

Say \hi{सुबह}, find the ṣ-b-ḥ root it shares with Arabic ṣabāḥ, and name the break from Sanskrit \hi{दिन} and \hi{रात}.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[subah]{\hi{सुबह} (subah) — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} and a root that also sits in Arabic}

\label{lesson:HI-C28-subah}



\begin{quote}
\hi{दिन} and \hi{रात} were both Sanskrit words, straight through. This one breaks that pattern completely — and lands on a root that also sits inside a different language entirely.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{सुबह} — a real surprise: not Sanskrit at all}
\textbf{\hi{सुबह}} (\textbf{subah}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{morning}\textquotedblright{} — is Hindi's everyday, ordinary word for morning. Unlike \textbf{\hi{दिन}} (\emph{din}) and \textbf{\hi{रात}} (\emph{raat}, both Sanskrit tatsama, met the last two lessons), \emph{subah} is genuinely \textbf{borrowed}: from \textbf{Persian} \textbf{\ar{صبح}} (\emph{subh}), itself from \textbf{Arabic} \textbf{\ar{صبح}} (\emph{ṣubḥ}), built on the Arabic triliteral root \textbf{\ar{ص}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ح}} (\emph{\textbf{ṣ-b-ḥ}}, \textquotedblleft{}dawn, to become morning\textquotedblright{}).

\subsection*{You'll want to know — A root that also sits inside an Arabic goodnight}
Here's the honest connection: this is the \textbf{exact same} Arabic root that sits inside the Arabic goodnight \textbf{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير}} (\emph{tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr}, \textquotedblleft{}good night,\textquotedblright{} literally \textquotedblleft{}may \textbf{you wake into goodness},\textquotedblright{} built on this very root). Hindi's everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} and Arabic's own good-night farewell — a phrase that never even mentions \textquotedblleft{}night\textquotedblright{} — both trace to the \textbf{same three Arabic consonants}, \ar{ص}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ح}, arriving in Hindi by a completely different route (via Persian) than they did staying in Arabic.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: din and raat didn't prepare you for this}
Don't assume every Hindi time-word will be Sanskrit just because \emph{din} and \emph{raat} were. \emph{Subah} is a genuine break in the pattern — a reminder that \textquotedblleft{}everyday Hindi word\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Sanskrit tatsama\textquotedblright{} aren't the same category, even when the last two examples made it look that way.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}subah\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}morning,\textquotedblright{} genuinely a Persian/Arabic loan
  \item the shared root — ṣ-b-ḥ, the same three consonants inside Arabic's tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr
  \item the honest break — unlike din and raat, subah is NOT Sanskrit
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \hi{सुबह} a Sanskrit tatsama, like \hi{दिन} and \hi{रात}? (\textbf{No} — a genuine Persian/Arabic loanword.) Which Arabic phrase, met earlier in this lesson, shares \hi{सुबह}'s exact root? (\textbf{\ar{تصبح} \ar{على} \ar{خير}}, \emph{tuṣbiḥ ʿalā khayr}, \textquotedblleft{}good night\textquotedblright{} — both trace to the Arabic root \ar{ص}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ح}, \emph{ṣ-b-ḥ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭha]{\hi{ठ} — the gap closed}

\label{lesson:HI-S143-letter-tha-retroflex}



\begin{quote}
Draw \textbf{\hi{ट}} once from memory, then look at it. Where is its gap?

Close that gap and you are most of the way to today's letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \hi{ठ}}
\textbf{\hi{ठ}} — \emph{ṭha}.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a short top-to-bottom central stem
  \item a separate counterclockwise \textbf{closed} round body
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{round body} & \textbf{stem} \\
\midrule
\hi{ट} & open at the upper right & part of the same run \\
\hi{ठ} & closed & drawn on its own first \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two differences, one you can hear and one you can only see: the body closes, and the stem stops being part of the body's run.

\subsection*{Script: the fifth breath pair}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{plain} & \textbf{breathy} \\
\midrule
\hi{त} & \hi{थ} \\
\hi{च} & \hi{छ} \\
\hi{ज} & \hi{झ} \\
\hi{प} & \hi{फ} \\
\textbf{\hi{ट}} & \textbf{\hi{ठ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Five pairs now. The puff of breath was learned once, a long way back, and every pair since has cost only a shape.

Words that were yours long before this page:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{ठीक}} — fine, all right
  \item \textbf{\hi{ठंड}} — cold
  \item \textbf{\hi{आठ}} — eight
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \hi{ठ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} draw the short central stem top-to-bottom
  \item \textbf{2.} lift at the stem's lower junction and sweep left, then counterclockwise around the closed round body back to the junction without lifting
  \item \textbf{3.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 2.} One more than \textbf{\hi{ट}}, and the extra lift is what lets the body close cleanly.

\begin{quote}
Verified three-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline; everyday handwriting may narrow or simplify the curve differently.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-\hi{ठ}-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these two words and say which letter each one carries
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\hi{रोटी}  ·  \hi{ठीक}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \hi{ठ} three times, saying \emph{ṭha} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Say it:} the one thing that tells the two round bodies apart
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What separates \textbf{\hi{ठ}} from \textbf{\hi{ट}} on the page? (The body closes.) How many pen lifts does it take? (Two.) Name the number you count to that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
